We first draw a picture of the situation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14188718/assets/417b284c87f735eb0c33f2369262b1548f9c54ff27ecbeb7880e91e9bc847f31.png)

Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =12+l+\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $12,$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<12.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ \sqrt{144-{l}^{2}} & =l \\ 144-{l}^{2} & ={l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =144 \\ {l}^{2} & =72 \\ l & =6\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=6\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,6\sqrt{2})$ | $6\sqrt{2}$ | $(6\sqrt{2},12)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $9$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=6\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6\sqrt{2}) & =12+6\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{144-(6\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =12+6\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{144-72} \\  & =12+6\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{72} \\  & =12+6\sqrt{2}+6\sqrt{2} \\  & =12+12\sqrt{2} \\  & =12(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
